# lab6_api_rerank.py -- Cohere Rerank v5 (+ relevant spans) and Voyage rerank-3
import cohere
import voyageai
from cohere import RerankRelevantSpans
from kb import TEXT
from evalkit import evaluate
from lab3_hybrid import hybrid_search
co = cohere.ClientV2()                    # reads CO_API_KEY
vo = voyageai.Client()                    # reads VOYAGE_API_KEY
def cohere_search(query: str, candidates: int = 20) -> list[str]:
    cand_ids = hybrid_search(query)[:candidates]
    resp = co.rerank(model="rerank-v5.0-pro", query=query, documents=[TEXT[i] for i in cand_ids],
                     top_n=10, max_tokens_per_doc=1024)
    return [cand_ids[r.index] for r in resp.results]
def voyage_search(query: str, candidates: int = 20) -> list[str]:
    cand_ids = hybrid_search(query)[:candidates]
    out = vo.rerank(query, [TEXT[i] for i in cand_ids], model="rerank-3", top_k=10)
    return [cand_ids[r.index] for r in out.results]
def compressed_context(query: str, keep: int = 3) -> list[str]:
    cand_ids = hybrid_search(query)[:20]
    docs = [TEXT[i] for i in cand_ids]
    resp = co.rerank(model="rerank-v5.0-pro", query=query, documents=docs, top_n=keep,
                     relevant_spans=RerankRelevantSpans(mode="enabled", threshold=0.3, max_spans=2))
    out = []
    for r in resp.results:
        spans = r.relevant_spans or []
        text = " ... ".join(docs[r.index][s.start:s.end] for s in spans) or docs[r.index]
        out.append(f"[{cand_ids[r.index]} {r.relevance_score:.2f}] {text}")
    return out
if __name__ == "__main__":
    q11 = "loyalty member: how long is the return window and when is the refund paid?"
    print("\n".join(compressed_context(q11)))
    evaluate("hybrid + Cohere v5 pro", cohere_search)
    evaluate("hybrid + Voyage rr-3", voyage_search)

context
max_tokens_per_doc=1024: the default is 4096. The docstring recommends no more than 1,000 documents per request.
cand_ids[r.index]: Cohere and Voyage return positions in YOUR list.voyageai.error.AuthenticationError: An API key is required for API-based models. Set your API key via the VOYAGE_API_KEY environment variable or pass it to the client (api_key=...).
v5 returns spans [start, end) in Unicode codepoints. Slice them: compression without a second LLM call. Spans need Rerank v5 or newer.
r.relevant_spans or []: no span, keep the full chunk. Do not call one vendor better from 15 queries.

This is the last step of Lab 4: the same 20 hybrid candidates go to two hosted rerankers, Cohere Rerank v5 and Voyage rerank-3. First point: both APIs return an index into the list you sent, so map it back with cand_ids[r.index], as in step 3, or every metric falls to the floor. The new part is relevant_spans: Cohere v5 marks the character ranges that answer the query, and slicing them drops the sentences the LLM does not need, with no second LLM call. Think of it as a highlighter pen: the reranker reads the page once and gives you only the marked lines. The numbers are illustrative and come from 15 queries, so do not call one vendor better from this run. A likely question is what happens when no span passes the threshold: relevant_spans is empty, and the code falls back to the full chunk. Hand-off: Lab 4 is complete; the next two slides collect the Qdrant and reranker mistakes that break these four steps.
Gotcha Qdrant 1.20

Qdrant fuses with k=2 by default, and a short prefetch returns nothing

northwind_rag/lab4_qdrant.py · server mode, changed lines · qdrant-client 1.20.0
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, models
client = QdrantClient(url="http://localhost:6333")       # integration tests: never only ":memory:"
assert client.info().version.startswith("1.20"), "client and server minor versions differ"
# docker run -p 6333:6333 qdrant/qdrant:v1.20.0          # the same server version as prod
# model, BGE_QUERY, create_collection and upsert: unchanged from Lab 4 step 2
def qdrant_hybrid(query: str, limit: int = 10, offset: int = 0, k_rrf: int = 60) -> list[str]:
    q_vec = model.encode_query(query, prompt=BGE_QUERY, normalize_embeddings=True).tolist()
    depth = limit + offset + 10                          # each prefetch >= limit + offset
    res = client.query_points(
        collection_name="northwind_kb",
        prefetch=[models.Prefetch(query=models.TextQuery(text=query), using="text", limit=depth),
                  models.Prefetch(query=q_vec, using="dense", limit=depth)],
        query=models.RrfQuery(rrf=models.Rrf(k=k_rrf, weights=[3.0, 1.0])),  # weights: server >= 1.17
        limit=limit, offset=offset)
    return [p.payload["chunk_id"] for p in res.points]
1 · The fusion constant SymptomYou switch engines and the rankings change. One list's top hit dominates. Causehybrid/fusion.py: DEFAULT_RANKING_CONSTANT_K = 2. The paper uses 60. With k=2, rank 1 scores 1/3 and rank 10 scores 1/12. With k=60 the curve is flat, so agreement between lists wins. FixPin Rrf(k=60) or your tuned k in code and in config review.
2 · The prefetch depth SymptomAn empty result, although both prefetches return points. CauseQdrant docs: the prefetch limit must be at least limit + offset of the main query, otherwise you can get an empty result. FixSet each prefetch limit ≥ limit + offset.
3 · Client and server versions (qdrant#8436) SymptomWeighted RRF fails: 400 - {"status":{"error":"Format error in JSON body: Expected some form of vector, id, or a type of query at line... CauseServer 1.13.2, client 1.17.x. Weighted RRF needs server v1.17.0+. Local ":memory:" mode also differs: it ignores a top-level query_filter on fusion with prefetches (#1372). FixPin client minor = server minor. Check client.info().version at startup. Run integration tests on qdrant/qdrant at the prod version.
Docs Hybrid and Multi-Stage Queries Issue qdrant#8436 Issues qdrant-client local mode
Three Qdrant defaults change hybrid results without any error, so check them before you trust a benchmark. First, Qdrant's RRF constant is 2, not the 60 from the paper: with k=2 the top hit of one list wins, as the worked example shows, where chunk A is first in BM25 only and still beats chunk B, which is fifth in both lists. Second, every prefetch must return at least limit plus offset points, or the main query can come back empty. Think of the prefetch as a funnel: if it is narrower than the bucket you want to fill, you get nothing out. Third, pin the client and server to the same minor version and test against a real server in Docker, because weighted RRF needs server 1.17 and local mode behaves differently. A likely question is whether k=60 is always right: no, tune k on your labelled set, but write the value down explicitly. Hand-off: the next slide shows the same kind of silent bug on the reranker side of Lab 4.
Gotcha Rerankers

Rerankers return positions and raw logits, not IDs or probabilities

northwind_rag/lab5_cross_encoder.py + lab6_api_rerank.py · the three fixes
import cohere, torch
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder
from kb import TEXT
from lab3_hybrid import hybrid_search

query = "zipper broke on my pack after 3 years"
cand_ids = hybrid_search(query)[:20]                     # business ids: 'c09', 'c08', ...
reranker = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2", max_length=512,
                        activation_fn=torch.nn.Sigmoid())   # 0-1 scores; default is Identity
co = cohere.ClientV2()                                   # reads CO_API_KEY

hits = reranker.rank(query, [TEXT[i] for i in cand_ids], top_k=10)
ranked = [cand_ids[h["corpus_id"]] for h in hits]        # positions -> business ids
resp = co.rerank(model="rerank-v5.0-pro", query=query,
                 documents=[TEXT[i] for i in cand_ids], top_n=10)
ranked = [cand_ids[r.index] for r in resp.results]       # index into YOUR list

store = ...                                              # your langchain_qdrant vector store
retriever = store.as_retriever(search_type="mmr",        # you want 0.9 relevance:
                               search_kwargs={"lambda_mult": 1 - 0.9})   # langchain-qdrant inverts it

rank() and rerank() return positions in the list you sent. Map them to IDs.

MiniLM-L6 returns logits. Add a Sigmoid, then tune any cut-off on labelled data.

langchain-qdrant sends lambda_mult as Qdrant's diversity. Pass 1 - 0.9.

SymptomAfter the reranker, every metric drops to near the floor (0.067-0.333). CauseThe code returned h["corpus_id"], an int 0-17: a position in the list you sent. FixMap back: cand_ids[h["corpus_id"]]. Cohere and Voyage r.index work the same way.
SymptomA cut-off score > 0.5 drops most good results. CauseThe model config sets Identity activation. rank() returns logits, about −11 to +11 (model card: [ 8.607138 -4.320078]). FixRank only, or pass activation_fn=torch.nn.Sigmoid(). Tune any "no answer" cut-off on labelled data, per model version. Cohere"It is not accurate to assume a score of 0.9 means the document is 2x more relevant than a document with a score of 0.45."
SymptomLangChain + Qdrant MMR with lambda_mult=0.9 ("mostly relevance") returns mostly diverse, less relevant chunks. Causelangchain_qdrant passes it as models.Mmr(diversity=...). Qdrant computes λ = 1 − diversity. FixPass 1 - desired, or call query_points with models.Mmr yourself.
Model card ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 Issue langchain#39052 (open)
Three reranker bugs that pass every unit test and only show up in the scorecard. First: CrossEncoder.rank, Cohere and Voyage all return the position in the list you sent, so if you return h["corpus_id"] you hand the evaluator ints 0-17 (the 18 candidates) and every metric falls to near the floor run; map through cand_ids. Second: ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 ships with an Identity activation, so the scores are logits from about -11 to +11, and a 0.5 cut-off on a logit is about 0.62 after a sigmoid, not a 50 percent threshold; pass activation_fn=torch.nn.Sigmoid() if you need 0-1, and tune any "no answer" cut-off on labelled data for each model version, because Cohere itself says a 0.9 is not twice as relevant as a 0.45. Third: langchain-qdrant passes lambda_mult straight into Qdrant's diversity, so 0.9 "mostly relevance" becomes mostly diversity; issue 39052 is still open, so pass 1 minus your value or call query_points with models.Mmr yourself. Analogy: the reranker gives you seat numbers and a raw thermometer reading, not passenger names and a percentage. Likely question: "Is a Cohere 0.9 a probability?" No; it is normalised to 0-1, but it is still a ranking signal. Hand-off: with the code bugs fixed, the next slide asks whether hybrid fusion and reranking help on every query.
arXiv Oct 2026

Hybrid wins on average and still hurts up to one query in five

arXiv 2610.30612 2026-10-22

The Fusion Tax: A Diagnostic Analysis of When Hybrid Retrieval Hurts

On 7 BEIR corpora the best fusion still ranks relevant documents below dense-only on 8-21% of queries. RRF is worse than dense-only on average on 5 of 7 corpora and wins only where both retrievers are balanced. A learned per-query router never beat static interpolation on held-out corpora.
Label 200-400 real queries. Count the four quadrants. Pick one static policy per corpus: interpolation α ≈ 0.6-0.7 when dense leads, RRF when balanced, or dense-only. Re-check when the corpus or encoder changes.
arXiv 2610.24341 2026-10-17 · Thomson Reuters

Optimal Fusion Weights Form Intervals, Not Points

74 of 128 dynamic fusion methods significantly beat standard RRF. The best weight for one query is an interval, not a point.
Tune one static weight first (github.com/thomsonreuters/query-based-rrf).
arXiv 2610.01324 2026-10-01

Evaluating Biomedical Reranking for LLM-Based Question Answering over Longitudinal Clinical Notes

Reranking lifted Hit@10 46.6% → 60.6% and MRR 0.2371 → 0.3252. Answer correctness rose only 44.8% → 48.6%.
Add an answer-level check after reranking.
Repo query-based-rrf
arXiv 2610.30612 Fusion Tax arXiv 2610.24341 WRRF intervals arXiv 2610.01324 Clinical rerank
This slide is the counterweight to the four steps of Lab 4: hybrid search wins on average, and you still have to check it query by query. The Fusion Tax paper sorts every query into four quadrants by which retriever finds a relevant document in its top 10; even the best fusion ranks relevant documents below dense-only on 8 to 21 percent of queries, and plain RRF is worse than dense-only on average on 5 of 7 BEIR corpora. The dots here are schematic, not the paper's counts. The Thomson Reuters paper shows that good fusion weights form an interval for each query, so one tuned static weight is the right first step, and their code is public. The clinical-notes study is the reranking version of the same lesson: Hit@10 rose 14 points, answer correctness rose under 4. Analogy: a team average can rise while two players get worse; you only see it in the per-player stats. Likely question: "So should I turn hybrid off?" No; measure it on 200 to 400 labelled queries from your own traffic and pick the policy per corpus. Blog Architecting and evaluating an AI-first search API (2025-09-25) Case Vespa: Perplexity
Perplexity's search API is the same shape as our Northwind pipeline at a much larger scale: 200 million queries a day over more than 200 billion URLs, served on Vespa. Step 1 is indexing: an ML model decides whether and when to index each URL, LLM-scored parsing rules improve in a loop, and documents are split into sub-document units. Steps 2 and 3 are the query path: hybrid lexical plus semantic retrieval for recall, prefilters, lexical and embedding scorers, then cross-encoders at document and sub-document level, and the LLM reads spans, which is exactly what Cohere relevant_spans gave us in Lab 4 step 4. The latency and quality numbers in step 4 are Perplexity's own measurements, so say "vendor claim" out loud. Analogy: a wide net first, then finer and finer sieves, and only the best grains reach the cook. Likely question: "Why not rerank everything with the cross-encoder?" Because it scores each query-document pair, so cost grows with the candidate count; cheap scorers cut the list first. Best practices

Retrieval rules: decide fusion per corpus, rerank 30-50, pin defaults

Do

  • Normalise IDs (E-4012, SKUs) on corpus and query. bm25s drops the 1-letter "E".
  • Choose fusion per corpus; keep dense-only as an option. 2610.30612
  • Pin the RRF k in code. Qdrant default 2, paper 60.
  • Fetch depth 20+ per retriever before fusion. Prefetch < limit + offset returns nothing.
  • Rerank 30-50 candidates when the LLM reads 10. 2609.27213
  • Replace MiniLM with Ettin-17M/32M; use bf16 + FlashAttention-2. NanoBEIR 0.6825 vs 0.6369.
  • Rank with reranker scores; tune cut-offs per model. MiniLM gives logits.
  • Score answers, not only MRR. Hit@10 +14 pts, answers +3.8 (2610.01324).

Don't

  • Add raw BM25 and cosine scores. The scales differ.
  • Trust only ":memory:" tests. Local Qdrant differs (#1372).
arXiv 2610.30612 arXiv 2609.27213 arXiv 2610.01324 Blog Ettin rerankers (2026-05-19)
northwind_rag/retrieval_config.py · sentence-transformers 6.2.0
# retrieval_config.py -- one reviewed config + the Ettin reranker
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder
from kb import TEXT
from lab3_hybrid import hybrid_search

RETRIEVAL = {                     # reviewed like code
    "fusion": "rrf",              # per corpus: Fusion Tax check
    "rrf_k": 60,                  # Qdrant default is 2
    "depth": 20,                  # per retriever, before fusion
    "rerank_candidates": 40,      # 30-50 when the LLM reads 10
    "keep": 10,
    "reranker": "cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-32m-v1",
}
reranker = CrossEncoder(RETRIEVAL["reranker"])   # HF Ettin blog, 2026-05-19

def retrieve(query: str, cfg: dict = RETRIEVAL) -> list[str]:
    cand_ids = hybrid_search(query, depth=cfg["depth"], k_rrf=cfg["rrf_k"])
    cand_ids = cand_ids[:cfg["rerank_candidates"]]
    hits = reranker.rank(query, [TEXT[i] for i in cand_ids], top_k=cfg["keep"])
    return [cand_ids[h["corpus_id"]] for h in hits]  # positions -> business ids
fusion rrf_k depth rerank_candidates keep reranker
These rules are the whole chapter in one reviewed config file. Steps 1 and 2 cover fusion: normalise codes so BM25 can see them, pick fusion per corpus because the Fusion Tax paper shows hybrid still hurts 8 to 21 percent of queries, and pin k because Qdrant's default is 2 while the paper uses 60. Step 3 covers reranking: BoundaryMORPH shows that a small rerank budget only re-checks the obvious top hits, so rerank 30 to 50 when the LLM reads 10, and the Ettin models from Hugging Face are both faster and better than MiniLM, as the throughput bars show. Step 4: reranker scores are for ranking, and the clinical-notes paper lifted Hit@10 from 46.6 to 60.6 percent while answer correctness moved only from 44.8 to 48.6, so measure the answer. Analogy: the config file is the recipe card; if a value is not written down, the next cook changes it without noticing. Likely question: "Why 40 candidates on an 18-chunk corpus?" Here the slice simply returns all 18; the value is for the production corpus, where the reranker budget must cover more than the 10 chunks the LLM reads. Hand-off: Chapter 5 keeps retrieve() on top of hybrid_search() and fixes the queries that still miss, such as q11 and q06.

Rewrite, contextualise or read it all: fix the queries that miss

Some misses are the query's fault, some are the chunk's, some are the window's.

Build 1 · q11 · Gemini 3.8 Flash · RAG-Fusion in 1 call Build 2 · q06 · Claude Haiku 5.5 · Contextual Retrieval Build 3 · parent-child · search small, return the policy arXiv Jul-Oct 2026 · gated rewrites, index-time work Northwind Outfitters · same 15 queries · evaluate() · on top of hybrid_search()
Chapter 5 keeps the Northwind Outfitters support assistant and the Chapter 4 hybrid_search(), and fixes the queries that still miss. Each miss has an owner. q11 asks two things in one sentence, so the query is at fault: one Gemini structured call writes paraphrases, a hypothetical answer and sub-questions. q06 asks about the tent warranty, but chunk c07 never says "tent", so the chunk is at fault: Claude Haiku 5.5 writes the missing context once at ingest, with prompt caching. Some answers need the whole policy page, so the window is at fault: parent-child retrieval searches small children and returns the full parent. Every change is scored with the same Chapter 1 evaluate() harness, and two paper slides show when to skip a rewrite and when to move the work to index time. Analogy: a librarian can rephrase your question, label the books better, or hand you the whole shelf, and each fix has a different cost. Likely question: "With a 1M-token window, why not read it all?" The last slide answers it: 2026 work selects evidence inside the long context too. Next: Build 1 fixes q11.

northwind_rag/lab7_query_transform.py · google-genai 2.33.0
from functools import lru_cache
from google import genai
from google.genai import types
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from evalkit import evaluate
from lab3_hybrid import dense_search, hybrid_search, rrf
client = genai.Client()                     # reads GEMINI_API_KEY / GOOGLE_API_KEY
class Rewrites(BaseModel):
    paraphrases: list[str] = Field(description="3 rewordings using policy vocabulary")
    hypothetical_answer: str = Field(
        description="2-sentence passage that would answer the question")
    sub_questions: list[str] = Field(
        description="1-3 self-contained sub-questions; 1 if the question is simple")
PROMPT = ("You rewrite customer-support questions for search over an outdoor retailer's "
          "policy KB (returns, refunds, warranty, payment error codes, shipping). "
          "Keep error codes exactly as written.\nQuestion: {q}")

@lru_cache(maxsize=1024)                    # never pay twice for the same query
def rewrite(query: str) -> Rewrites:
    resp = client.models.generate_content(
        model="gemini-3.8-flash", contents=PROMPT.format(q=query),
        config=types.GenerateContentConfig(
            response_mime_type="application/json", response_schema=Rewrites,
            thinking_config=types.ThinkingConfig(thinking_level="LOW")))
    return resp.parsed

def fusion_search(query: str) -> list[str]:
    rw = rewrite(query)
    lists = [hybrid_search(query)]          # always keep the original query
    lists += [hybrid_search(p) for p in rw.paraphrases + rw.sub_questions]
    lists.append(dense_search(rw.hypothetical_answer, 20))  # HyDE: dense only
    return rrf(lists, k=60, weights=[2.0] + [1.0] * (len(lists) - 1))
evaluate("hybrid", hybrid_search)
evaluate("RAG-Fusion (MQ+HyDE+decomp)", fusion_search)

This build fixes q11, "loyalty member: how long is the return window and when is the refund paid?", which needs two chunks: c04 for the 60-day loyalty window and c02 for the 5-7 day refund. One Gemini 3.8 Flash call with a Pydantic response_schema and the JSON MIME type returns three paraphrases, a two-sentence hypothetical answer and one to three sub-questions; thinking is LOW and an lru_cache means a repeated question costs nothing. fusion_search keeps the original query at weight 2.0, because the September SPLADE-v3 study (2609.37911) found gains in every setting that keeps at least 30% of the weight on the original query, and it sends the HyDE passage to the dense side only, because SAFE-QE (2610.13810) counted 57.5 invented terms per query for HyDE. The illustrative result moves R@3 from 0.867 to 0.933 and R@5 from 0.933 to 0.967, at the cost of one LLM call and five to seven retrievals per query; the ranks in the animation are illustrative too. Analogy: you ask the question three ways and split it in two, but you still listen most to the customer's own words. Likely question: "Should every query go through this?" No: gate it to multi-part, vague or very short queries, skip it when the query holds an exact code like E-4012, check that every CODE.findall(query) code survives in each rewrite, and fall back to the original query when resp.parsed is None. arXiv Jul–Oct 2026 · query rewriting

Rewrite only when a cheap signal says the first pass is weak

arXiv 2610.13810 9 Oct 2026 · SAFE-QE

LLM query expansion injects hallucinated terms

Unsupported terms per query: HyDE 57.5, Query2doc 27.8, SAFE-QE 4.3, at equal nDCG@10. On a strong learned sparse retriever, every expansion method regresses.
Send HyDE to the dense side only. Filter expansion terms.
arXiv 2609.05637 4 Sep 2026 · EMNLP Industry

Better Together: complementary rewriting, strong baseline

On BGE + cross-encoder + MMR, one rewriter is at best on par. A union of rewriters: +12.5 HIT@10 (51.70 vs 39.22, 512K docs). A score gate keeps +4.3 and rewrites <40% of queries. AmbigNQ: −2.4.
Union of rewriters behind a gate. Rerank on the original query.
arXiv 2607.23121 25 Jul 2026 · Snap SMART

LLM-augmented hybrid retrieval for product ads

Rule queries on BM25 win retargeting. LLM queries on dense ANN win prospecting. A light gate sends about 10% of users to the LLM path: −90% LLM cost, +27.6% conversion in a 2-week A/B test.
Route by difficulty. Pay for the LLM only on hard queries.
arXiv 2610.13810 arXiv 2609.05637 arXiv 2607.23121
Three papers from the last three months say that query rewriting is not free and does not always help. SAFE-QE counted 57.5 unsupported terms per query for HyDE against 4.3 for its filtered method at equal nDCG@10, which is why Build 1 sends the HyDE passage to the dense side only. Better Together shows that on a strong baseline one rewriter is at best on par, a union of rewriters gives +12.5 HIT@10, and a score gate keeps +4.3 of that while it rewrites fewer than 40% of queries; the rewritten pool is always reranked against the original question. Snap's SMART paper shows the same gate in production: about 10% of users take the LLM path, LLM cost falls by 90% and ad conversion rises 27.6% in a two-week A/B test. Analogy: a triage nurse sends only the unclear cases to the specialist. Likely question: "What is the gate signal?" Use a cheap first-pass signal such as the top-1 reranker score, and tune tau on your labelled set, not on the test queries. Build: Claude Haiku 5.5 writes each chunk's missing context once

northwind_rag/lab8_contextual.py · anthropic 2.3.0
import json, os, anthropic
from kb import CHUNKS, doc_text
from evalkit import evaluate
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
DOCUMENT_CONTEXT_PROMPT = "\n<document>\n{doc_content}\n</document>\n"
CHUNK_CONTEXT_PROMPT = """
Here is the chunk we want to situate within the whole document
<chunk>
{chunk_content}
</chunk>

Please give a short succinct context to situate this chunk within the overall document \
for the purposes of improving search retrieval of the chunk.
Answer only with the succinct context and nothing else.
"""
def situate(doc: str, chunk: str) -> str:
    resp = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-5-5", max_tokens=300,
        output_config={"effort": "low"},                  # no temperature: 400 on API 2026-10-21
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
            {"type": "text", "text": DOCUMENT_CONTEXT_PROMPT.format(doc_content=doc),
             "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},     # same doc for every chunk -> cache it
            {"type": "text", "text": CHUNK_CONTEXT_PROMPT.format(chunk_content=chunk)}]}])
    u = resp.usage
    print(f"  cache_write={u.cache_creation_input_tokens}"
          f" cache_read={u.cache_read_input_tokens} in={u.input_tokens}")
    return next(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text").strip()
CACHE = "contexts.json"
ctx = json.load(open(CACHE)) if os.path.exists(CACHE) else {}
for cid, did, text in CHUNKS:                              # document order keeps the cache warm
    if cid not in ctx:
        ctx[cid] = situate(doc_text(did), text)
json.dump(ctx, open(CACHE, "w"), indent=1)
ctext = [f"{ctx[cid]}\n{text}" for cid, _, text in CHUNKS]  # index this for BM25 AND dense
# omitted (8 lines): re-index ctext in bm25s + bge-small; contextual_hybrid(q) = rrf(k=60)
evaluate("contextual hybrid", contextual_hybrid)

Cookbook Enhancing RAG with Contextual Retrieval arXiv 2610.10170
Query q06 asks when the tent warranty starts, but chunk c07 only says "the window starts on the purchase date", so BM25 and the embedder both rank it low. Contextual Retrieval fixes the chunk, not the query: Claude Haiku 5.5 reads the whole document plus one chunk, writes a one-line context, and we index context plus chunk in BM25 and in the dense index alike. The cache meter stays at zero because our toy documents are under Haiku 5.5's 512-token cache minimum and the API returns no error; on real policy PDFs you should see cache_write on the first chunk and cache_read after it. Analogy: a librarian writes a short shelf label on each loose page so that it can be found again. Likely question: "Is the LLM call worth it at $0.10 per million input tokens?" Run the free control first, the heading path prefix, which arXiv 2610.10170 found better than LLM-contextualised windows on its corpora. SymptomThe pasted cookbook cell messages.create(..., temperature=0.0) fails. Causeanthropic 2.3.0 messages.create has no temperature. SDK 2.0.0 (2026-10-21) adds API version 2026-10-21: temperature, top_p or top_k returns a 400 error on every model. FixDelete it. Set output_config={"effort": "low"} (low..max, default medium).
SymptomAttributeError: 'ThinkingBlock' object has no attribute 'text' CauseHaiku 5.5 runs adaptive thinking by default. content[0] can be a thinking block. FixTake the first block with type == "text".
Symptomcache_read_input_tokens stays 0 on real documents. No error. CausePrefix under the minimum (512 tokens on Haiku 5.5, 4,096 on the cookbook's claude-haiku-4-5), a change before the breakpoint, or > 5 min between chunks of one document. FixDocument first and unchanged, its chunks back-to-back, or "ttl": "1h". Alert when a real document never caches.
Cookbook Enhancing RAG with Contextual Retrieval Docs Prompt caching
The Contextual Retrieval cookbook is the right recipe, but its notebook cell rots on the current SDK, so engineers who paste it lose an afternoon. First, anthropic 2.3.0 has no temperature parameter, and API version 2026-10-21 rejects temperature, top_p and top_k with a 400 on every model; effort is the control that remains, and low is enough for a one-line chunk context. Second, Haiku 5.5 thinks by default, so content[0] can be a thinking block: always pick the first block whose type is text. Third, prompt caching fails silently: below 512 tokens on Haiku 5.5, or 4,096 on the cookbook's Haiku 4.5, or when chunks of one document are more than five minutes apart, you just pay full price, so log an alert when a real document never writes or reads the cache. Analogy: a recipe that still says "gas mark 4" in a kitchen with an induction hob. Likely question: "Why not pin the old SDK?" You can for a week, but the old API version is the one that goes away, so fix the call. Next: Build 3, the third fix, returns the whole policy parent.

northwind_rag/lab9_parent_child.py · embed children, return parents
from langchain_classic.retrievers import ParentDocumentRetriever
from langchain_core.documents import Document
from langchain_core.embeddings import Embeddings
from langchain_core.stores import InMemoryStore
from langchain_core.vectorstores import InMemoryVectorStore
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from kb import DOCS, QUERIES, DOC_OF, doc_text

class STEmbeddings(Embeddings):                            # 6-line adapter, avoids langchain-huggingface pin
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.m = SentenceTransformer(name)
    def embed_documents(self, texts: list[str]) -> list[list[float]]:
        return self.m.encode_document(texts, normalize_embeddings=True).tolist()
    def embed_query(self, text: str) -> list[float]:
        return self.m.encode_query(text, prompt="Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: ",
                                   normalize_embeddings=True).tolist()

retriever = ParentDocumentRetriever(
    vectorstore=InMemoryVectorStore(STEmbeddings("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5")),
    docstore=InMemoryStore(),
    child_splitter=RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=160, chunk_overlap=0, separators=["\n", ". "]),
    search_kwargs={"k": 12},                                # BEFORE: missing -> similarity_search k=4
)
parents = [Document(page_content=doc_text(d), metadata={"doc_id_biz": d}) for d in DOCS]
retriever.add_documents(parents, ids=list(DOCS))            # parent ids = D1..D4
hits = mrr_sum = 0.0
for qid, (text, gold_chunks) in QUERIES.items():
    gold_docs = {DOC_OF[c] for c in gold_chunks}
    got = [d.metadata["doc_id_biz"] for d in retriever.invoke(text)]
    hits += bool(set(got[:1]) & gold_docs)
    mrr_sum += next((1 / r for r, d in enumerate(got, 1) if d in gold_docs), 0.0)
    print(f"{qid} gold={sorted(gold_docs)} got={got}")
print(f"parent-level Hit@1={hits / len(QUERIES):.3f}  MRR={mrr_sum / len(QUERIES):.3f}")

arXiv 2610.10170 · −0.033 arXiv 2610.07091 · hit@1 68.6% Repo langchain_classic
Parent-child (small-to-big) retrieval embeds small children for a precise match and hands the model the whole parent, here the full Northwind policy document, so q11 gets the 60-day loyalty window and the 5-7 day refund rule together and c07 arrives under its "Warranty Policy: Tents" title. The trap is the order of operations: ParentDocumentRetriever runs similarity_search for k children first and only then de-duplicates to parents, and InMemoryVectorStore defaults to k=4, so four children from one policy collapse into one parent; ask for about three children per parent you want. Install langchain-classic, not langchain-huggingface[full], because that extra pins sentence-transformers below 6 and pip downgrades or fails. The price is context: each parent is 5-10 times the tokens of a child, and the October 2026 ablation 2610.10170 found that naive two-stage hierarchical retrieval hurts, while structure-aligned chunks help, so make the parent a real policy section and cap it so 3-5 parents fit the budget. Analogy: you search the index cards, but you hand the reader the whole chapter. Likely question: "Why not just use bigger chunks?" Big chunks blur the embedding; small children keep the match sharp, and the parent keeps the answer complete. Next: three papers that move this kind of work to index time.

Hypothetical Prompt Embeddings (HyPE)

At index time, generate the questions each chunk answers. Embed the questions and point them at the chunk. Up to +42 pts context precision and +45 pts claim recall on six datasets.
Move HyDE-style work to ingest. Reuse the Rewrites schema as "questions this chunk answers".
arXiv 2608.20845 21 Aug 2026

RAG Deserves an Index: Why Ingest-Time Compilation Beats Query-Time Interpretation

Quote-verified claims gave 85.2% correct at ~2.2k reader tokens vs 72.5% at 16.3k for the best chunking. Only contextual hybrid + rerank kept pace, at ~21x the tokens. Updates 33.7x cheaper.
For high-read corpora, compile claims at ingest. Drop each claim whose quote does not match the source.
arXiv 2610.08463 6 Oct 2026 · NVIDIA

UNREAL: Unifying Retrieval and Long-Context with a Single Model

One frozen LLM selects evidence from a 21M-chunk index and from inside a long prompt. Long context and RAG become one selection step.
"Long context or RAG?" has a third answer: retrieve inside the long context and drop distractors first.
These three papers move work out of the query path. Step 1: HyPE asks an LLM once, at index time, for the questions each chunk answers, so q06 matches the question "purchase or delivery date?" and the paper reports up to 42 points more context precision with no LLM call per query. Step 2: "RAG Deserves an Index" compiles quote-verified claims at ingest; it reached 85.2% at about 2.2k reader tokens against 72.5% at 16.3k for the best chunking, and only a contextual-chunk hybrid plus rerank stack kept pace, at about 21 times the tokens. Step 3: NVIDIA's UNREAL uses one frozen LLM to select evidence both from a 21M-chunk index and from inside a long prompt, so long context and RAG become the same selection step. Analogy: a library that writes the index cards when a book arrives, not when a reader asks. Likely question: "Is HyPE the same as HyDE?" No: HyDE writes a fake answer per query at query time; HyPE writes questions per chunk once, at ingest. Next: Chapter 6 (Lab 5) puts the choice of retrieval path behind a router in an ADK workflow.
06

Agentic RAG with ADK 2.x: route, retrieve, verify, retry

An agent earns its latency only where a route or a retry changes the answer.

google-adk 2.13.0 · Workflow router → 3 branches separate verifier gate IT: KB first, web second MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3
Lab 5 · Northwind People & IT helpdesk Repo ADK Workflow Routing Sample @ v2.13.0 Paper Corrective RAG (CRAG), arXiv 2401.15884
Chapter 6 is Lab 5: we build the Northwind People and IT helpdesk as an ADK 2.13.0 Workflow graph, step by step. The animation shows the whole lab in one loop: a message enters the router, and an HR question runs retrieve_hr, grader, answerer and a separate verifier; when the first retrieval is weak, a routed back-edge rewrites the query and the attempt badge goes from 1/3 to 2/3; an IT question goes to it_triage, which searches the known-issues KB first; a pizza order gets a polite refusal. The point of the lede is cost: every agent step adds latency and tokens, so we add a route or a retry only where it changes the answer. Analogy: a hospital triage desk sends each patient to one ward, and a second doctor signs off before discharge. Likely question: "Why not one big agent with all the tools?" Because a graph keeps the budget, the order of tools and the verifier in code, where you can test them; the Dropbox case later in this chapter shows the other side of that trade-off.
Lab 5 Northwind helpdesk · step 1 of 4

Functions and agents are nodes; state flows by parameter name

lab5_helpdesk.py · step 1: nodes and state
import asyncio, os, re
from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from google.adk import Agent, Event, Workflow
from google.adk.runners import InMemoryRunner

MODEL = os.getenv("MODEL", "gemini-3.8-flash")
HR_DOCS = {
    "PTO-2026": "Full-time staff accrue 1.75 PTO days per month. "
                "At most 5 unused PTO days carry over into the next year.",
    "PARENTAL-2026": "Birth and adoptive parents get 16 weeks of paid leave after 90 days of employment.",
    "REMOTE-2026": "Staff may work remotely up to 3 days per week with manager approval. "
                   "Working abroad over 30 days needs HR approval.",
}

class Route(BaseModel):
    category: Literal["hr_policy", "it_support", "out_of_scope"]

class Verdict(BaseModel):
    supported: bool = Field(description="True only if EVERY claim in the draft is stated in the evidence")
    unsupported_claims: list[str] = Field(description="Claims of the draft not found in the evidence")

def take_question(node_input: str):
    return Event(state={"question": node_input})

router = Agent(name="router", model=MODEL, output_schema=Route, output_key="route",
               instruction="Classify this employee message: {question}")

def route_on_category(node_input: Route):
    yield Event(route=node_input.category)

def retrieve_hr(question: str, k: int = 2):
    words = set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+", question.lower()))
    ranked = sorted(HR_DOCS.items(), key=lambda kv: -len(words & set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+", kv[1].lower()))))
    return Event(state={"evidence": "\n".join(f"[{d}] {t}" for d, t in ranked[:k])})

The code is step 1 of lab5_helpdesk.py, the one file that the whole lab grows, adapted from the ADK Workflow Routing sample, and every node here is either a plain function or an Agent. Walk the four bands: the imports and the three HR policy documents; take_question writes the question into session state with Event(state=...); the router agent returns JSON that ADK validates against Route and stores as a dict under route, and route_on_category gets a Route object back through its type hint and picks the edge with Event(route=...); retrieve_hr gets question from state only because its parameter has that name. Analogy: state is a shared whiteboard, and each function reads the boxes whose labels match its parameter names. Likely question: "What if I rename the parameter to query?" Then ADK finds no state key with that name and raises WorkflowDataError, which is the gotcha later in this chapter. Next, step 2 wires these nodes into a graph.
Lab 5 Northwind helpdesk · step 2 of 4

Declare the graph as edges: a chain, a route map, a second chain

lab5_helpdesk.py · step 2: the edges
# step 1: imports, MODEL, take_question, router, route_on_category, retrieve_hr
# step 3 defines: answerer, verifier, gate (the HR chain, next slide)

it_agent = Agent(name="it_agent", model=MODEL,
                 instruction="Give a 2-line IT first-aid tip for: {question}")
def refuse():
    yield Event(message="I can only help with HR policy and IT questions.")

root_agent = Workflow(name="hr_helpdesk", edges=[
    ("START", take_question, router, route_on_category),
    (route_on_category, {"hr_policy": retrieve_hr,
                         "it_support": it_agent,
                         "out_of_scope": refuse}),
    (retrieve_hr, answerer, verifier, gate),
])

async def main():
    runner = InMemoryRunner(node=root_agent)
    for i, q in enumerate(["How many PTO days can I carry over into 2027?",
                           "Can you book me a pizza?"]):
        await runner.run_debug(q, session_id=f"s{i}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

This is step 2 of Lab 5: lab5_helpdesk.py now turns the nodes from step 1 into a graph with three edge tuples. it_agent is a placeholder that step 4 replaces with it_triage, and the three HR-chain nodes answerer, verifier and gate are the subject of the next slide. Walk the bands: the first tuple is a chain from "START" through take_question and router to route_on_category; the dict tuple is a conditional edge map, and the key comes from Event(route=...); the third tuple chains retrieve_hr, answerer, verifier and gate, and Workflow validates the whole graph in model_post_init. The token shows the run: the pizza message takes the out_of_scope edge and stops at refuse, the PTO question runs the whole HR chain to gate. Analogy: the edges list is a railway timetable, and route_on_category is the switch operator who throws one lever per train. Likely question: "Why InMemoryRunner(node=...)?" Because a Workflow is a BaseNode, not a BaseAgent, so agent= is the wrong slot; agent= and node= are mutually exclusive, and agent-only code paths raise the TypeError on the card.

lab5_helpdesk.py · step 3: the HR chain
# Agent, Event, MODEL and Verdict come from step 1
answerer = Agent(name="answerer", model=MODEL, output_key="draft",
                 instruction="Answer: {question}\nUse ONLY this evidence and "
                             "cite ids like [PTO-2026]:\n{evidence}")

verifier = Agent(name="verifier", model=MODEL, output_schema=Verdict,
                 output_key="verdict",
                 instruction="Evidence:\n{evidence}\n\nDraft:\n{draft}\n\n"
                             "Check each claim of the draft against the evidence.")

def gate(node_input: Verdict, draft: str):
    if node_input.supported:
        yield Event(message=f"VERIFIED: {draft}")
    else:
        yield Event(message="Opened HR ticket; could not verify: "
                            f"{node_input.unsupported_claims}")

output_key="draft" writes the answer. {evidence} reads state.

The verifier sees only evidence and draft: the node default is include_contents='none'.

gate gets the Verdict as node_input and the draft by name.

One unsupported claim keeps the gate shut. Verify with a different model. Log how often the router picks each branch.

arXiv 2609.35774 Post-generation verification arXiv 2607.24010 When should Active RAG retrieve?
This is step 3 of Lab 5: the three nodes that the HR-chain edge from step 2 names after retrieve_hr. The answerer writes its text to state["draft"] through output_key, and its {question} and {evidence} placeholders read state. The verifier is a separate agent that sees only {evidence} and {draft}, because a workflow node defaults to include_contents='none', and it returns a Verdict; gate reads that Verdict as node_input and the draft by parameter name, so only verified text reaches the employee, which is the check_identity pattern of the agent_in_workflow sample. In the last step the draft carries a planted claim, "and 3 more days with manager approval", that no evidence sentence supports, so the gate stays shut and an HR ticket opens. Analogy: the answerer writes the memo, the verifier is the colleague who reads only the memo and the policy page, never the chat. Likely question: "Why not let the answerer check itself?" A separate agent, ideally on a different model, does not share the writer's blind spots; arXiv 2609.35774 found a post-generation completeness check (d = +0.48) beats agentic search tweaks, and 2607.24010 says to log how often the router picks each branch, because router quality changes with the traffic mix. Next, step 4 replaces the it_agent placeholder with a real IT triage agent.
Lab 5 Northwind helpdesk · step 4 of 4

IT branch: search the known-issues KB first, Google Search second

lab5_it_triage.py · step 4: the IT branch
import asyncio, os, re
from google.adk import Agent
from google.adk.runners import InMemoryRunner
from google.adk.tools.google_search_agent_tool import GoogleSearchAgentTool, create_google_search_agent
MODEL = os.getenv("MODEL", "gemini-3.8-flash")
KNOWN_ISSUES = {
    "KI-311": "Okta SSO login loop after a password reset. Fix: clear the stale session cookie "
              "and re-sync the SAML clock skew. Queue: identity. Severity P2.",
    "KI-207": "Claim PDF upload fails for files over 20 MB. Fix: compress or split the PDF. "
              "Queue: claims-tools. Severity P3.",
}
def search_known_issues(query: str) -> dict:
    """Searches Northwind's internal known-issues knowledge base.
    Args:
      query: Keywords from the ticket, e.g. error text and product area.
    Returns:
      A dict with 'results': a list of {'id', 'text'} for matching known issues."""
    words = set(re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", query.lower()))
    hits = [{"id": k, "text": v} for k, v in KNOWN_ISSUES.items()
            if len(words & set(re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", v.lower()))) >= 2]
    return {"status": "ok", "results": hits}            # [] is an answer, not an error
web_search = GoogleSearchAgentTool(create_google_search_agent(MODEL))   # tool name: google_search_agent
it_triage = Agent(name="it_triage", model=MODEL, tools=[search_known_issues, web_search],
    instruction="""You triage Northwind IT tickets. Ticket: {question?}
1. ALWAYS call search_known_issues first.
2. Call google_search_agent ONLY if no internal issue matches (e.g. a vendor outage).
3. Reply exactly: Severity: P1-P4 | Queue: ... | Why: ... with citations [KI-xxx] or the web page title.""")
async def main():
    runner = InMemoryRunner(agent=it_triage, app_name="it_triage")
    for i, t in enumerate(["I'm stuck in an Okta login loop since my password reset",
                           "Zoom will not start for anyone in the office, is Zoom down today?"]):
        for e in await runner.run_debug(t, session_id=f"t{i}", quiet=True):
            if e.author == "it_triage" and e.content and e.content.parts and e.content.parts[0].text:
                print("ANSWER:", e.content.parts[0].text)
            if e.grounding_metadata and e.grounding_metadata.grounding_chunks:
                for c in e.grounding_metadata.grounding_chunks:
                    if c.web: print("  web source:", c.web.title)
if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main())   # import-safe for lab5_helpdesk.py

A plain function is a tool. ADK reads its signature and docstring. No match returns results: [], not an error.

google_search cannot share a request with function tools. The wrapper sets propagate_grounding_metadata=True.

The instruction fixes the order: KB first, web only on no match. Then lab5_helpdesk.py imports it: "it_support": it_triage.

Web sources arrive in grounding_chunks[i].web.title. Show the Search suggestions (renderedContent).

output · illustrative

This is step 4 of Lab 5, the last lab step before the build: the IT branch gets a real triage agent, and the Workflow route map now says "it_support": it_triage instead of it_agent. Step 1: search_known_issues is a plain Python function; ADK builds the tool declaration from its signature and Google-style docstring, and it returns an explicit empty list when nothing matches, so the model sees "no match", not an error. Step 2: google_search is a Gemini built-in that cannot share a request with function tools, so GoogleSearchAgentTool wraps it in a search-only sub-agent and carries the grounding metadata back up. Think of a librarian who checks the in-house binder first and phones the outside reference desk only when the binder is silent. Step 4: the code prints web.title from the grounding chunks, and production UIs must also render the Search suggestions. The {question?} placeholder gives it the ticket from state when it runs as a Workflow node, and renders empty when you run this file alone. Likely question: "Why not put google_search straight into the tools list?" Because the docs say it can only be used by itself; the wrapper also gives you one sub-agent that you can rate-limit, log and switch off per tenant. That completes the three branches; the next slide makes the HR branch retry a weak search.
Build · Lab 5 Northwind helpdesk · HR back-edge

Build: a routed back-edge retries weak retrieval at most 3 times

lab5_helpdesk.py · HR branch with a back-edge · google-adk 2.13.0
# steps 1-3: imports, MODEL, HR_DOCS, router, route_on_category, refuse, answerer, verifier, gate
from lab5_it_triage import it_triage              # step 4: the IT branch
MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3                                  # the budget lives in code, not in the prompt
class Grade(BaseModel):                           # 3-way grade, as in arXiv 2610.22652
    label: Literal["correct", "ambiguous", "incorrect"] = Field(
        description="correct: evidence fully answers; ambiguous: partly; incorrect: irrelevant")
    missing: str = Field(description="What the evidence is missing, or ''")
def take_question(node_input: str):               # now also seeds query and attempts
    return Event(state={"question": node_input, "query": node_input, "attempts": 0})
def retrieve_hr(query: str, attempts: int):       # replaces retrieve_hr(question, k=2)
    q = set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+", query.lower()))
    scored = sorted(((len(q & set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+", t.lower()))), d, t)
                     for d, t in HR_DOCS.items()), reverse=True)
    hits = [f"[{d}] {t}" for s, d, t in scored[:2] if s >= 2]   # can return nothing
    return Event(state={"evidence": "\n".join(hits) or "(no results)", "attempts": attempts + 1})
grader = Agent(name="grader", model=MODEL, output_schema=Grade, output_key="grade",
               instruction="Question: {question}\nEvidence:\n{evidence}\nGrade the evidence.")
def decide(node_input: Grade, attempts: int):
    if node_input.label == "correct":
        yield Event(route="answer")
    elif attempts >= MAX_ATTEMPTS:
        yield Event(route="abstain")
    else:
        yield Event(route="rewrite", state={"missing": node_input.missing})
rewriter = Agent(name="rewriter", model=MODEL, output_key="query",
    instruction="Query '{query}' failed; missing: {missing}. Write ONE better keyword "
                "query for an HR policy manual for: {question}. Output only the query.")
def abstain(question: str, attempts: int):
    yield Event(message=f"Opened an HR ticket after {attempts} searches: '{question}'.")
root_agent = Workflow(name="hr_helpdesk", edges=[
    ("START", take_question, router, route_on_category),
    (route_on_category, {"hr_policy": retrieve_hr, "it_support": it_triage, "out_of_scope": refuse}),
    (retrieve_hr, grader, decide),
    (decide, {"answer": answerer, "rewrite": rewriter, "abstain": abstain}),
    (answerer, verifier, gate),                   # the verifier gate from step 3 stays
    (rewriter, retrieve_hr),                      # the corrective back-edge
])

Predicting Partial Answer Quality and Utility in Agentic RAG

Answer quality plateaus early. Early stopping cut about 11% of the iterations at about 98% of the quality.

This build adds Corrective RAG style self-correction to the HR branch of the Northwind helpdesk, in the same lab5_helpdesk.py: take_question now also seeds query and attempts, and retrieve_hr now reads query instead of question. Step 1: the first try loops decide straight back to retrieve_hr, and ADK rejects it when it builds the graph, because a cycle needs at least one routed edge. Steps 2 and 3: retrieve_hr can return "(no results)" and counts the attempt; the grader gives a 3-way grade; decide mixes that grade with a hard budget of 3 kept in code; the rewriter's output_key overwrites state["query"], so "Lisbon for six weeks" becomes "working abroad over 30 days HR approval" and attempt 2 finds REMOTE-2026, which still goes through the verifier gate. Analogy: a librarian who rephrases your request at most three times and then opens a ticket for a human. The gotcha is real: pass the whole grade dict into the rewriter prompt and the loop never recovers, so pass only the missing part. Likely question: "Why 3 and not 10?" The September paper shows quality plateaus early: early stopping cut about 11% of iterations and kept about 98% of quality. Next: the three ADK errors you hit while you wire this graph.

ADK fails on missing state keys, and its default model is unlisted

The answerer has no output_key="draft", or the name is misspelled. FixMatch output_key to the parameter name, or give the parameter a default.

import os
from google.adk import Agent, Event
from google.adk.tools.google_search_agent_tool import (
    GoogleSearchAgentTool, create_google_search_agent)
# Verdict, retrieve_hr, verifier and the edges: unchanged from steps 1-3 and the build

MODEL = os.getenv("MODEL", "gemini-3.8-flash")     # not DEFAULT_MODEL 'gemini-3.5-flash'
web_search = GoogleSearchAgentTool(create_google_search_agent(MODEL))   # search alone

answerer = Agent(name="answerer", model=MODEL, output_key="draft",   # matches gate(draft)
                 instruction="Answer: {question}\nUse ONLY this evidence and "
                             "cite ids like [PTO-2026]:\n{evidence?}")

def gate(node_input: Verdict, draft: str = ""):    # default: no WorkflowDataError
    if node_input.supported and draft:
        yield Event(message=f"VERIFIED: {draft}")
    else:
        yield Event(message="Opened HR ticket; could not verify: "
                            f"{node_input.unsupported_claims}")

{evidence?} renders empty when a route skips retrieve_hr.

output_key equals the parameter name, and the default stops the crash.

Set model= from config. Keep google_search in its own agent.

Repo ADK Workflow Routing Sample Docs Gemini models Docs ADK Google Search
Three errors that every team hits in the first hour with ADK 2.13 workflows. First, an agent instruction like {evidence} is a hard dependency on session state: if a route reaches the answerer before retrieve_hr has written the key, ADK raises "Context variable not found"; write the key earlier, or add a question mark, the same syntax the workflows/loop sample uses for {feedback?}. Second, function-node parameters bind from state by name, so gate(draft) needs an upstream output_key="draft"; a typo gives WorkflowDataError, and a default value keeps the gate safe because it still refuses an empty draft. Third, ADK 2.13.0 ships DEFAULT_MODEL 'gemini-3.5-flash', an ID the Gemini models page does not list, so always pass model from config, and never put google_search next to a function tool in one agent, which gives HTTP 400. Analogy: state keys are function arguments that the type checker cannot see, so you test the routes, not only the happy path. Likely question: "Why not make every placeholder optional?" Because then a missing evidence key silently produces an answer with no evidence; use the question mark only on routes where an empty value is correct, and keep the verifier gate. arXiv 2609.16453 · partial answer quality arXiv 2607.24010 · when to retrieve arXiv 2610.22652 · evidence gate
These three papers from the last three months test the design choices we just built into the Northwind workflow. The first one shows that agentic RAG answer quality usually flattens before the loop stops by itself: stopping early cut about 11% of iterations and kept about 98% of the quality, so a hard MAX_ATTEMPTS of 3 with a grader-owned stop is a sound budget, not a shortcut. The second paper finds that retrieval can hurt answers and that a simple uncertainty or retrieval-score trigger often matches a learned router, and the winner changes from dataset to dataset; the animation swaps the two bars for that reason, so log realized usage and harm rate for each route. The third paper, from consumer banking, adds a middle outcome, "related mismatch", between answer and no answer, and with hybrid retrieval and a cross-encoder raised Top-1 from 50.48% to 79.05%, but on only 210 queries, so treat it as a strong hint, not a benchmark. Analogy: a good librarian says "we have a book about X, not Y" instead of "nothing found". Likely question: "Should we train a router?" Start with a score threshold, measure harm per route on your own traffic, and train a router only if it beats the threshold there. Blog Knowledge graphs, MCP and DSPy in Dash (2026-01-28) Blog Context engineering in Dash (2025-11-17) Blog Building Dash (2025-04-24)
Dropbox Dash is a work search and chat product over many third-party apps, and its team measured what our IT branch is about to face. Step 1 is the race: an agent with one MCP tool per app needed up to 45 seconds for a simple query, while the same question against Dash's own index came back within seconds; the timeline on the slide is schematic, only the 45 seconds is their number. Step 2 shows why the index wins: connectors crawl apps and their ACLs, content becomes markdown with metadata and embeddings, the knowledge graph ships as bundles through the normal index, and a hybrid BM25 plus dense store with multi-pass ranking sits behind one super tool that replaced 5 to 10 retrieval tools. Step 3: they treat the judge as a product, starting at 8 percent disagreement with humans and lowering it with explanations, o3, RAG as a judge and DSPy. Analogy: a library catalogue beats phoning every bookshop in town. Likely question: "So is MCP bad?" No, the Dash MCP server itself exposes one tool; the lesson is fewer, better retrieval tools, which is why our Lab 5 agent searches the KB first and keeps web search in one sub-agent. Next: the chapter rules in one checklist and one config file.
Best practices

Agentic RAG rules: budgets in code, isolated verifiers, empty results

Do

  • Keep the attempt budget in state plus a route. Prompts do not stop loops.
  • Let retrieval return "(no results)". Else the grader never sees failure.
  • Verify with another agent and model on {evidence} + {draft} only.
  • Set model ids from config; pin google-adk==2.13.0. DEFAULT_MODEL is unlisted.
  • KB first, web second, web in GoogleSearchAgentTool. Switch off per tenant.
  • Add abstain and related-mismatch routes. Top-1 50.48% → 79.05% (2610.22652).
  • Log route usage and harm rate. 2607.24010
  • Add loops only where routes earn latency. ~90 s vs ~8-9 s (2610.14428).

Don't

  • Mix google_search with File Search or RAG Engine in one request. HTTP 400.
  • Let the generator decide when to stop. 2609.16453

# helpdesk_config.py -- one reviewed place for every budget and model id
import os

MODEL = os.getenv("MODEL", "gemini-3.8-flash")
VERIFIER_MODEL = os.getenv("VERIFIER_MODEL", "gemini-4-argon")  # != MODEL
MAX_ATTEMPTS = int(os.getenv("MAX_ATTEMPTS", "3"))   # then abstain
RETRIEVE_MIN_OVERLAP = 2  # below this, retrieve_hr returns "(no results)"
WEB_FALLBACK_TENANTS = {"northwind-it"}  # may use the web sub-agent
ROUTES = ("hr_policy", "it_support", "out_of_scope")

def log_route(route: str, counts: dict[str, int]) -> None:
    assert route in ROUTES, route
    counts[route] = counts.get(route, 0) + 1  # realized usage, weekly review
This slide turns Lab 5 into rules you can check in a code review, and every rule lands as a badge on the helpdesk graph. Step 1: the attempt budget and the "(no results)" floor live in code, because a model can ignore a limit that exists only in its prompt, and a retriever that always returns something never lets the grader say "nothing found". Step 2: the verifier is a separate agent on a separate model that sees only evidence and draft, and every model id comes from config, because ADK 2.13.0's default model is not on the Gemini models page. Steps 3 and 4: web search sits behind its own sub-agent that you can switch off per tenant, there are explicit escape routes, and you log how often each route fires, because the July paper shows router rankings change with the traffic mix. Analogy: the config file is the cockpit checklist; the pilot does not decide fuel limits mid-flight. Likely question: "Why not just use a skills agent like Airbnb?" You can, when the work tolerates it: their agent matched human procedure 99.2% of the time, but each case took about 90 seconds against 8 to 9 for the fixed pipeline. Next chapter: when one retrieval is not enough, Lab 6 builds multi-hop search agents for the Acme Outfitters supplier-compliance desk.
07

Search agents: plan the hops, track sources, gate the answer

Multi-hop questions fail at the hop nobody logged. Lab 6 keeps a register: one row per sub-question, with its answer, source id and retry count.

split one question into linked hops every answer carries a source id no answer while a hop is open
Chapter 7 is Lab 6: an Acme Outfitters compliance analyst asks who must approve a return of the jacket made by the supplier that failed the March 2026 audit, and no single passage answers that. The animation shows the whole lab: the planner splits the question into three linked sub-questions, each hop fills one register row with an answer and a source id (AUD-1, SUP-4, RET-2), and the gate under the register stays closed until all three rows are filled. The register is simply a table with one row per sub-question: the question, the answer, the source id and the retry count. The lede is the failure attribution finding of this quarter (arXiv 2608.20627): a hop-1 retrieval error shows up as a wrong answer at hop 3, so we log every hop. Analogy: a detective's case board, where every pinned fact has its evidence tag and nobody names the suspect while a card is still blank. After the lab, we scale the desk with 2026 papers on rank-first discovery (arXiv 2607.26497), search as code (OpenSaC, arXiv 2610.25779), RL-trained search agents, and PayPal's SCOUT MCP gateway (arXiv 2608.23992). The register idea comes from arXiv 2610.21184, Beyond Retrieval Failure. Likely question: "Why not let one ReAct agent search freely?" Because free search drifts away from the open sub-question; the register keeps every search tied to one named requirement. Next: the first Lab 6 slide sets up the store and the planner.
Lab 6 Acme Outfitters compliance desk · step 1 of 3

Plan the hops: sub-questions that reference earlier answers as #1

lab6/lab6_multihop_register.py · part 1 of 3
import os
from typing import TypedDict
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from langchain_core.documents import Document
from langchain_core.vectorstores import InMemoryVectorStore
from langchain_google_genai import ChatGoogleGenerativeAI, GoogleGenerativeAIEmbeddings
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
llm = ChatGoogleGenerativeAI(model=os.getenv("MODEL", "gemini-3.8-flash"))
PASSAGES = [
    ("AUD-1", "Kestrel Textiles failed the March 2026 audit and is on audit hold."),
    ("AUD-2", "Bluefin Gear passed the March 2026 audit with no findings."),
    ("SUP-4", "Kestrel Textiles manufactures the TrailLite rain jacket."),
    ("SUP-5", "Bluefin Gear manufactures the Summit fleece."),
    ("RET-2", "Returns from a supplier on audit hold need the Quality Lead, Priya Natarajan."),
    ("RET-1", "Standard returns are approved automatically by the returns portal.")]
store = InMemoryVectorStore(GoogleGenerativeAIEmbeddings(model="gemini-embedding-001"))
store.add_documents([Document(t, metadata={"id": i}) for i, t in PASSAGES])
class Plan(BaseModel):
    subquestions: list[str] = Field(description=
        "2-4 single-fact sub-questions in order; refer to earlier answers as #1, #2")
class Hop(BaseModel):
    answer: str = Field(description="Short answer, or UNKNOWN if the passages do not state it")
    source_id: str = Field(description="Id of the passage that states the answer, or ''")
class State(TypedDict, total=False):       # total=False: a key may be missing
    question: str; register: list[dict]; hops: int; answer: str   # row: {q, a, src, tries}
def plan(s: State):
    p = llm.with_structured_output(Plan).invoke(
        f"Decompose into single-fact sub-questions: {s['question']}")
    return {"register": [{"q": q, "a": None, "src": None, "tries": 0}
                         for q in p.subquestions], "hops": 0}

This is my own implementation of the training-free requirement register from arXiv 2610.21184, not the paper's code. Analogy: a detective writes every open question on the case board before the first interview, and leaves a blank for each name that is not known yet. Likely question: "Why plan up front instead of letting the agent search freely?" Because free search drifts away from the open sub-question. Next: hop() resolves the rows one at a time.
Lab 6 Acme Outfitters compliance desk · step 2 of 3

Resolve one hop at a time: substitute answers, widen k on a miss

lab6/lab6_multihop_register.py · part 2 of 3
# part 1 (previous slide): imports, llm, PASSAGES, store, Plan, Hop, State, plan()
from typing import Literal
def hop(s: State):
    reg = [dict(r) for r in s["register"]]                       # new list: never mutate s
    i = next(n for n, r in enumerate(reg) if r["a"] is None)      # first open requirement
    q = reg[i]["q"]
    for n, r in enumerate(reg[:i], 1):                            # rows resolve in order,
        q = q.replace(f"#{n}", r["a"])                             # so each #n has an answer
    docs = store.similarity_search(q, k=2 + 2 * reg[i]["tries"])  # widen k on retry
    ctx = "\n".join(f"[{d.metadata['id']}] {d.page_content}" for d in docs)
    res = llm.with_structured_output(Hop).invoke(f"Passages:\n{ctx}\nSub-question: {q}")
    reg[i].update(q=q, tries=reg[i]["tries"] + 1)
    if res.answer != "UNKNOWN" and res.source_id:
        reg[i].update(a=res.answer, src=res.source_id)
    return {"register": reg, "hops": s["hops"] + 1}
# hop again while a row is open and hops < 2 x rows; at the cap, answer() refuses
def next_step(s: State) -> Literal["hop", "answer"]:
    still_open = any(r["a"] is None for r in s["register"])
    return "hop" if still_open and s["hops"] < 2 * len(s["register"]) else "answer"

hop() builds a new list and never mutates s. next() picks the first open row.

#1 becomes Kestrel Textiles. k=2 returns AUD-1 and SUP-5: UNKNOWN, so tries = 1.

Retry: k = 2 + 2 × 1 = 4. SUP-4 is now in the passages, so the row resolves with a source_id.

Row 3 resolves. No row is open, so next_step returns "answer" after 4 of 6 hops.

arXiv 2610.21184The register is its training-free idea. This code is my own version.
arXiv 2608.20627Post-hoc diagnosis finds hop-1 faults (0.91), but 0.00 at hops 2-3. Log the register at every hop.
This slide runs the hop loop of Lab 6, one hop per click, and the second hop misses on purpose so you see the retry. First, hop() builds a new list from the register so it never mutates the input state in place; it returns the new list, and LangGraph's default reducer replaces the register key with it, while keys that a node does not return keep their values. next() then picks the first open row. Second, the hop-1 answer, Kestrel Textiles, replaces #1; rows resolve in order, so every #n already has an answer when it is substituted, and with at most 4 sub-questions there is no #10 to confuse with #1. In this run the k=2 search returns AUD-1 and SUP-5, the model says UNKNOWN, and tries goes to 1. Third, the retry widens k to 2 + 2 × 1 = 4, SUP-4 is now in the passages, and the row resolves with tries 2. Fourth, row 3 resolves and next_step returns answer after 4 hops; the cap is 2 × 3 = 6, and at the cap the answer node refuses, which is the next slide. The output is illustrative: your run may hit SUP-4 at k=2. Analogy: a relay race where each runner must hand over a signed baton. Likely question: "Why not let the model rephrase on a miss?" Widening k is cheaper and deterministic. arXiv 2608.20627 shows why we log the register at every hop: post-hoc coverage diagnosis finds hop-1 faults 91 percent of the time but none at hops 2 and 3, so later-hop faults are invisible after the fact.
Lab 6 Acme Outfitters compliance desk · step 3 of 3

Refuse to answer while any sub-question is still open

lab6/lab6_multihop_register.py · part 3 of 3
# parts 1-2: imports, llm, store, Plan, Hop, State, plan(), hop(), next_step()
def answer(s: State):
    open_q = [r["q"] for r in s["register"] if r["a"] is None]
    if open_q:                                                   # sufficiency gate
        return {"answer": f"Cannot answer yet; unresolved: {open_q}"}
    chain = "\n".join(f"{r['q']} -> {r['a']} [{r['src']}]" for r in s["register"])
    prompt = (f"Using only this evidence chain, answer: {s['question']}\n"
              f"{chain}\nCite every id used.")         # answers only, no passage text
    return {"answer": llm.invoke(prompt).text}
g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node(plan); g.add_node(hop); g.add_node(answer)
g.add_edge(START, "plan"); g.add_edge("plan", "hop")
g.add_conditional_edges("hop", next_step, ["hop", "answer"])   # path list
g.add_edge("answer", END)
app = g.compile()
if __name__ == "__main__":
    q = ("Who must approve a return of the jacket made by the supplier "
         "that failed the March 2026 audit?")
    out = app.invoke({"question": q}, {"recursion_limit": 20})   # worst case: 10 steps
    for r in out["register"]:
        print(r)
    print("\nANSWER:", out["answer"])

This slide closes Lab 6 with the gate, the compiled graph and the run. Step 1 is the real run: 4 hops, because row 2 needed one retry, then every row holds a source id, the gate opens and the model cites AUD-1, SUP-4 and RET-2. Be clear about what the answer model sees: only the extracted q, a and source strings, not the passage text, so this is extraction plus formatting, not verified synthesis; to let the model check the citations, add the passage text for each src to the chain. In langchain-core 1.x, .text on the message is a property. Step 2: the path list in add_conditional_edges lets LangGraph check and draw the targets; draw_mermaid returns Mermaid text, so print it and paste it into any Mermaid viewer. Step 3: each node run is one super-step. This run is plan, 4 hops and answer, 6 steps; the worst case for the largest plan of 4 sub-questions is plan 1, plus the hop cap of 2 × 4, plus answer 1, which is 10, so recursion_limit 20 leaves room. Step 4 is a what-if, not this run: if row 3 keeps returning UNKNOWN, next_step loops to the cap of 6 hops and answer() refuses with the open sub-question instead of a guess. That targets arXiv 2610.21184: the register cut wrong answers with missing evidence from 382 to 234 of 1,000 MuSiQue questions, but premature answers rose, so the bottleneck moves to checking sufficiency. Analogy: an auditor does not sign the report while one line on the checklist is blank. Likely question: "How do I debug a wrong multi-hop answer?" Log out["register"] per request; it shows which hop failed and whether retrieval or reasoning failed, the split that arXiv 2609.33778 studies. A variation for later: rows with no #n can run in parallel with langgraph.types.Send. Next: three LangGraph traps that hit this exact graph.
Gotcha langgraph 1.2.17

LangGraph now allows 10,007 steps: set recursion_limit and a counter

lab6/lab6_guards.py · langchain 1.4.7 · langgraph 1.2.17
from typing import Literal
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model          # langchain==1.4.7 (Lab 6 pins)
# importing Lab 6 builds its 6-passage store; hop() and answer() keep Lab 6's llm
from lab6_multihop_register import Plan, State, hop, answer
# without the "google_genai:" prefix, a gemini-* name infers google_vertexai
llm = init_chat_model("google_genai:gemini-3.8-flash")      # used by plan() below
def plan(s: State):
    p = llm.with_structured_output(Plan).invoke(
        f"Decompose into single-fact sub-questions: {s['question']}")
    subqs = p.subquestions or [s["question"]]                # avoids StopIteration in hop()
    return {"register": [{"q": q, "a": None, "src": None, "tries": 0} for q in subqs], "hops": 0}
def next_step(s: State) -> Literal["hop", "answer"]:
    still_open = any(r["a"] is None for r in s["register"])
    under_cap = s.get("hops", 0) < 2 * len(s["register"])       # optional key: use .get
    return "hop" if still_open and under_cap else "answer"
g = StateGraph(State); g.add_node(plan); g.add_node(hop); g.add_node(answer)
g.add_edge(START, "plan"); g.add_edge("plan", "hop")
g.add_conditional_edges("hop", next_step, ["hop", "answer"]); g.add_edge("answer", END)
app = g.compile()
q = ("Who must approve a return of the jacket made by the supplier "
     "that failed the March 2026 audit?")
out = app.invoke({"question": q}, {"recursion_limit": 20})       # default is now 10007
Repo langgraph @ 1.2.17 · _internal/_config.py Docs Build a custom RAG agent
1 · The loop has no real ceiling SymptomA hop loop with no exit makes thousands of LLM calls. CauseThe default limit is now 10007, not 25. FixRoute on hops. Pass {"recursion_limit": 20} as the safety net.
2 · The provider is inferred SymptomRequests go to Vertex AI and fail with auth errors. CauseA bare gemini-* name infers google_vertexai. FixAdd the google_genai: prefix, or use ChatGoogleGenerativeAI.
3 · Empty plans and missing keys SymptomStopIteration in hop(), or KeyError: 'hops'. CauseThe plan is empty. total=False never fills a missing key. FixFall back to [question]. Read optional keys with s.get().
In langgraph 1.2.17 the default recursion limit is 10007, read from LANGGRAPH_DEFAULT_RECURSION_LIMIT in _internal/_config.py, not 25. So Lab 6's hop loop without its counter does not fail fast when a row never resolves: it can burn thousands of LLM calls first. With a limit you get an error such as "langgraph.errors.GraphRecursionError: Recursion limit of 20 reached without hitting a stop condition. You can increase the limit by setting the recursion_limit config key." Treat the hops counter as the real guard and the recursion limit as the safety net: the cap is 2 times the register length, and recursion_limit 20 sits above the worst case of 10 steps. The chart in panel 1 is on a log scale; 25 and 10,007 are about 400 times apart. The second trap is init_chat_model with a bare Gemini name: it infers google_vertexai and warns "Inferred model_provider='google_vertexai' from ... This default will change to 'google_genai' in the next major release." Pass the google_genai prefix, or use ChatGoogleGenerativeAI as Lab 6 does. The guard file needs langchain 1.4.7, which the Lab 6 install line already pins; the new llm applies to plan() only, because hop() and answer() keep Lab 6's ChatGoogleGenerativeAI, which already talks to the Gemini API. Importing the Lab 6 module also builds its store, which costs six embedding calls. The third trap is an empty plan: next() finds no open row and raises StopIteration; and TypedDict with total=False never fills missing keys, so s["hops"] raises KeyError: 'hops' if a node reads it before plan() wrote it. Fall back to the question and read optional keys with get. Analogy: a fuse in the wall is the safety net, but you still switch off the heater when the room is warm. arXiv Jul–Sep 2026 · ranked discovery

Rank first, then let the agent reason over the ranked list

arXiv 2607.264972026-07-29

BM25 Wins at Scale: A Scaling Study of RAG Paradigms

A file-system agent (an LLM that browses files with ls and grep) wins on small corpora. BM25 wins from ~10M tokens.
Keep BM25 next to vectors. Hand the agent a ranked list.
lab6/rank_first.py · bm25s 0.3.15 · Lab 6 store
import bm25s
from lab6_multihop_register import PASSAGES, store
IDS = [i for i, _ in PASSAGES]
bm25 = bm25s.BM25(k1=1.2, b=0.75)
bm25.index(bm25s.tokenize([t for _, t in PASSAGES], stopwords="en"))
def rrf(rankings, k=60):                     # Lab 4: fuse ranks, not scores
    fused = {}
    for ranking in rankings:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            fused[doc_id] = fused.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(fused, key=fused.get, reverse=True)
def ranked(q: str, k: int = 4) -> list[str]:   # the agent starts from this list
    toks = bm25s.tokenize(q, stopwords="en")
    docs, _ = bm25.retrieve(toks, corpus=IDS, k=min(k, len(IDS)))
    dense = [d.metadata["id"] for d in store.similarity_search(q, k=k)]
    return rrf([list(docs[0]), dense])[:k]
print(ranked("Which jacket does Kestrel Textiles make?"))
also 2608.01913Accuracy tracks cumulative gold recall@25 (r = 0.99). 77.5-93.6% of search episodes add no new evidence.
also 2609.14412Split the first search into clues, retrieve per clue, union, rerank: 83.1% → 90.5% on BrowseComp-Plus.
The main point comes from BM25 Wins at Scale (arXiv 2607.26497): an agent should reason over a ranked list, not replace ranking. The paper grows one enterprise corpus, EnterpriseRAG-Bench, through 28 nested tiers from 1.7 million to 601 million tokens. A file-system agent, an LLM that browses the documents with ls and grep tools, leads on the smallest tiers; at about 10 million tokens BM25 overtakes it and leads every larger tier, ending near 20 points ahead, while the agent spends 39 times the query tokens. The line shapes in the chart are schematic; the crossover, the margin and the cost ratio are the paper's numbers. The paper also measures dense retrieval, which is efficient but less accurate, and graph RAG, which hits construction-cost walls before deployment scale; I left those lines out to keep one comparison. The code applies the lesson to the Acme desk: index the Lab 6 passages with bm25s, fuse BM25 and dense ranks with the Lab 4 RRF, and let hop() start from that list. Two more papers point the same way. 2608.01913: accuracy follows cumulative gold recall@25, the share of gold passages seen in the top 25 results so far, at r = 0.99, and 77.5 to 93.6 percent of search episodes, where an episode is one search call and its results, add no new evidence; so log new evidence per step and pivot on a repeated query. 2609.14412, Question's Gambit: split the first search into clues, retrieve per clue, union and rerank; accuracy goes from 83.1 to 90.5 percent with the retriever unchanged. Analogy: a librarian hands you the ten best books first; you do not walk every shelf. Likely question: "Does this mean agents are useless at scale?" No; the agent still does the reasoning, but it starts from ranked discovery. Next: let the agent write its searches as code.

# ReAct: one tool call per action; every result lands in the context

lab6/deep_research_cell.py · after: the agent writes this cell
# OpenSaC runs the cell; only printed output becomes an observation
from opensac import sdk

queries = ["EU PFAS restriction textiles", "PFAS ban outdoor jackets EU"]
pool = sdk.search(queries, limit=10)         # rankings fused locally, one limit
if pool:
    best = sdk.rerank(queries[0], pool[:100], top_n=min(3, len(pool)))
    doc = sdk.content.fetch(best[0].url)     # the page stays in Python
    print(best[0].url, doc.text[:800])       # a bounded extract for the model

Before: each search or fetch costs one model turn. Every result enters the context.

sdk.search sends both reformulations and fuses the rankings locally under one limit.

Rerank and fetch run in the sandbox. pool, best and doc stay Python variables.

Only the URL and an 800-character extract enter the context. One cell is one turn.
